¶ '''unmaze''' (un-māz′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''maze.''] To relieve from terror or bewilderment. [Rare.] {{smaller block|This poor Arpinate . . .
''Unmaz’d'' us, and took pains for all the town. {{right|''Stapylton'', tr. of Juvenal, viii. 312.}}}} '''unmeaning''' (un-mē′ning), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having no meaning or signification: as, ''unmeaning'' words. —'''2.''' Not having or not indicating intelligence or sense; mindless; senseless; expressionless. ''Byron'', To Thyrza. '''unmeaningly''' (un-mē′ning-li), ''adv.'' In an unmeaning manner; without meaning or sense. '''unmeaningness''' (un-mē′ning-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unmeaning. ''Miss Burney'', Camilla, iii. 1. '''unmeant''' (un-ment′), ''a.'' Not meant; not intended; undesigned. {{smaller block|But Rhœtus happened on a death ''unmeant.'' {{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, x. 561.}}}} '''unmeasurable''' (un-mezh′ṳ̄r-a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unmesurable''; < ''un-''1 + ''measurable.''] Immeasurable. {{smaller block|Glotonye is ''unmesurable'' appetit to ete or to drynke. {{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}} Their ''unmeasurable'' vanity. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, v. 2.}}}} '''unmeasurableness''' (un-mezh′ṳ̄r-a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unmeasurable. [Rare.]
readings.c1s3:
¶
'''unmeddling''' (un-med′ling), ''a.'' Not meddling; not interfering with the concerns of others; not officious. ''Chesterfield.''

'''unmeddlingness''' (un-med′ling-nes), ''n.'' Forbearance of interposition, or of busying one’s self with something. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|If then we be but sojourners, . . . here must be an . . . ''unmeddlingness'' with these worldly concernments.
{{right|''Bp. Hall.''}}}}

'''unmedicinable''' (un-mē-dis′in-a̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Powerless to cure.
{{smaller block|<poem>Away with his ''vnmedcinable'' balme
Of worded breath : forbear, friends, let me rest.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Gentleman Usher, iv. 1. (''Davies.'')}}}}
'''2.''' That cannot be cured.
{{smaller block|<poem>But these, much-med′cine-knowing men, physicians, may recure,
Thou yet ''unmed′cinable'' still.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xvi. 24. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unmeditated''' (un-med′i-tā-ted), ''a.'' Not meditated; not prepared by previous thought; unpremeditated. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Fit strains pronounced, or sung
''Unmeditated.''</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 149.}}}}

'''unmeek†''' (un-mēk′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unmeke'', ''unmek'', ''unmeoc''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''meek''.] '''1.''' Not meek or gentle; fierce; cruel; harsh; severe.
{{smaller block|An ''unmeke'' lord.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iv. meter 7.}}}}
'''2.''' Not kind; disdainful.
{{smaller block|She to me was nought ''unmeke''.
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 590.}}}}

'''unmeet''' (un-mēt′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unmet'', < AS. ''ungemet'', immoderate, immense, mixed with ''un-''
readings.c1s4: ''mete, unmaite'', < AS. ''unmǣte'' (= OHG. ''unmāzi'', MHG. ''unmāze'', ''unmæze'', immoderate), < ''un-'', not, + ''mǣte'', moderate: see ''meet''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Not meet or fit; improper; not suitable; unbecoming.
readings.c2s1:
{{smaller block|<poem>The Ladie, hearkning to his sensefull speach,
Found nothing that he said ''unmeet'' nor geason.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. iv. 37.}}
<poem>White Angel of the Lord! ''unmeet''
That soil accursed for thy pure feet.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', The Peace of Europe.}}}}
'''2†.''' Unseemly; coarse; rustic.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hir voice ful clere was ful and swete,
She was nought rude ne ''unmete.''</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 752.}}}}
'''3.''' Not suited or fitted; not adapted.
{{smaller block|Ah Maud, you milk-white fawn, you are all ''unmeet'' for a wife.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud.}}}}

'''unmeetly''' (un-mēt′li), ''adv.'' Not fitly; improperly; unsuitably; unworthily.
{{smaller block|A faire mayden . . . upon a mangy jade ''unmeetly'' set.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. vi. 16.}}}}

'''unmeetness''' (un-mēt′nes), ''n.'' Unfitness; unsuitableness; unbecomingness.
{{smaller block|Vast ''unmeetness'' in marriage.
{{right|''Milton'', Divorce, i. 13.}}}}

'''unmellowed''' (un-mel′ōd), ''a.'' Not mellowed; not fully matured; not toned down or softened by ripeness or length of years.
{{smaller block|His head ''unmellow’d'', but his judgement ripe.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 4. 70.}}}}

'''unmelodious''' (un-me-lō′di-us), ''a.'' Not melodious; wanting melody; harsh.
{{smaller block|The ''unmelodious'' noise of the braying mules.
{{right|''Sir T. Herbert.''}}}}

'''unmelodiousness''' (un-me-lō′di-us-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unmelodious.

'''unmentionable''' (un-men′sho̤n-a-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being mentioned; unworthy of or unfit for being mentioned, named, or noticed.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''unmercifully''' (un-mėr′si-fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In an unmerciful manner; without mercy or tenderness; cruelly; often, especially in colloquial use, extremely; very: as, ''unmercifully'' cold weather.
{{smaller block|<poem>Full fiercely layde the Amazon about,
And dealt her blowes ''unmercifully'' sore.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. vii. 31.}}}}

'''unmercifulness''' (un-mėr′si-fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unmerciful; cruelty; inhumanity.

'''unmeritable†''' (un-mer′i-ta̤-bl), ''a.'' Having no merit or desert; worthless.
{{smaller block|<poem>This is a slight ''unmeritable'' man,
Meet to be sent on errands.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iv. 1. 12.}}}}

'''unmerited''' (un-mer′i-ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not merited; not deserved; obtained without service or equivalent: as, ''unmerited'' promotion. ''Milton'', P. L., xii. 278.—'''2.''' Not deserved because of wrong-doing; cruel; unjust: as, ''unmerited'' sufferings or injuries; an ''unmerited'' disgrace.

'''unmeritedness''' (un-mer′i-ted-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unmerited.
{{smaller block|The freeness and ''unmeritedness'' of God’s grace.
{{right|''Boyle'', Works, I. 278.}}}}

'''unmeriting''' (un-mer′i-ting), ''a.'' Not meriting; not meritorious or deserving.
{{smaller block|A brace of ''unmeriting'', proud, violent, testy magistrates.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 1. 47.}}}}

'''unmerry''' (un-mer′i), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unmerie, unmurie''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''merry''.] Not merry; not disposed to mirth.
readings.c3s1:
{{smaller block|Ther slepeth ay this god ''unmerie.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 74.}}}}

¶
'''unmeted''' (un-mē′ted), ''a.'' Not meted or measured. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Some little of the anxiety I felt in degree so ''unmeted.''
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Villette, xxxix. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unmethodical''' (un-me-thod′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' Not methodical.

'''unmethodized''' (un-meth′ọd-īzd), ''a.'' Not methodized or regulated by method, system, or plan; not systematized. ''J. Harington'', Oceana, p. 12.

'''unmetrical''' (un-met′ri-ka̤l), ''a.'' Not metrical; irregular in meter.

'''unmevable†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''unmovable.''

'''unmew''' (un-mū′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''mew''<sup>4</sup>.] To set free as from a mew; emancipate; release. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>But let a portion of etherial dew
Fall on my head, and presently ''unmew''
My soul; that I may dare, in wayfaring,
To stammer where old Chaucer used to sing.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Endymion, i.}}}}

'''unmighty†''' (un-mī′ti), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unmighty'', ''unmyghty'', ''unmigty'', < AS. ''unmihtig'', ''unmehtig'' (= OHG. ''unmahtig''), < ''un-'', not, + ''mihtig'', mighty.] Powerless; incapable of success.
{{smaller block|He . . . is ''unmyghty'' for his shrewednesse.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 858.}}}}

'''unmild†''' (un-mīld′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unmilde'', < AS. ''unmilde'' (= OHG. ''unmilt''), < ''un-'', not, + ''milde'', mild.] Not mild; harsh; severe. ''Gower'', Conf. Amant., i.
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''unmildness†''' (un-mīld′nes), ''n.'' Want of mildness; harshness. ''Milton'', Divorce, ii. 7.

'''unmilitary''' (un-mil′i-tạ̄-ri), ''a.'' Not according to military rules or customs; not of a military character.

'''unminded''' (un-mīn′ded), ''a.'' Not minded; not heeded; not kept in mind. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|A poor, ''unminded'' outlaw sneaking home.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iv. 3. 58.}}
<poem>Where was your gratitude, who in your coffers
Hoarded the rusty treasure which was due
To my ''unminded'' father?</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, v. 1.}}}}

'''unmindful''' (un-mīnd′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not mindful; not heedful; not attentive; regardless; heedless; careless: as, ''unmindful'' of laws; ''unmindful'' of health or of duty.
{{smaller block|''Unmindful'' of the crown that virtue gives.
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 9.}}
<poem>For not ''unmindful'' of thee are the Gods; . . .
Even here they seek thee out, in Hela’s realm.</poem>
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Balder Dead.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' Careless, inattentive (to), heedless, unobservant, negligent, forgetful, unheedful.}}

'''unmindfully''' (un-mīnd′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In an unmindful manner; carelessly; heedlessly.

'''unmindfulness''' (un-mīnd′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' Heedlessness; inattention; carelessness.

'''unmingle''' (un-ming′gl), ''v. t.'' To separate, as things mixed. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It will ''unmingle'' wine from the water, the wine ascending and the water descending. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}}

'''unmingleable''' (un-ming′gl-a-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be mingled or mixed. [Rare.]

That cannot be mingled or mixed. [Rare.] {{smaller block|The property of oil being ''unmingleable'' with water. {{right|''Boyle'', Works, I. 536.}}}} '''unmingled''' (un-ming′gld), ''a.'' Not mingled; not mixed; unmixed; unalloyed; pure: as, to view some event with ''unmingled'' dread. {{smaller block|Springs on the tops of high hills are . . . pure and ''unmingled.'' {{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 396.}}}} '''unmiraculous''' (un-mi-rak′ū-lus), ''a.'' Not miraculous. ''Young'', Night Thoughts, ix. '''unmiraculously''' (un-mi-rak′ū-lus-li), ''adv.'' In an unmiraculous manner; without a miracle. '''unmiry''' (un-mīr′i), ''a.'' Not miry; not muddy; not foul with dirt. [Rare.] {{smaller block|With safe ''unmiry'' feet. {{right|''Gay'', Trivia, iii.}}}} '''unmistakable''' (un-mis-tā′ka-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be mistaken or misunderstood; clear; evident. Also ''unmistakeable.'' {{smaller block|Not the Scripture, but ''unmistakeable'' and indefectible oral tradition, was the rule of faith. {{right|''Tillotson.''}}}} ={{smaller|'''Syn.''' Palpable, manifest, obvious, patent, unequivocal, unambiguous, decided.}} '''unmistakably''' (un-mis-tā′kạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an unmistakable manner; so as not to be mistaken. Also ''unmistakeably.'' {{smaller block|She went first to the best adviser, God— Whose finger ''unmistakably'' was felt In all this retribution of the past. {{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, i. 116.}}}} '''unmiter, unmitre''' (un-mī′tėr), ''v. t.'' To deprive of a miter; degrade or depose from the rank and dignity of a bishop. ''Milton.'' [Rare.]
